Analysis of electricity and water end-uses in university campuses:
case-study of the University of Bordeaux in the framework of the
Ecocampus European Collaboration☆
Jean-Franc¸ois Bonnet *, Christophe Devel, Patrick Faucher, Jacques Roturier
Ecocampus Group, University of Bordeaux 1, 351 cours de la Liberation, 33405 Talence Cedex, France
Received 1 January 2001; accepted 9 April 2001
Abstract
In large university campuses, electricity and water uses are similar to those of medium-sized cities, as demonstrated by the
Ecocampus European Collaboration. The diversity of activities and energy end-uses can be considered as signiﬁcant as in a city
where residential, commercial and industrial uses are present. The main goal of the paper is to deﬁne and implement a tool allowing
to address the diversity of activities and end-uses when analysing energy demand and environmental impact on a campus. Electricity
and water uses on the campus of University of Bordeaux were studied, with support of both the French Electricity Utility and the
Regional Water Utility Commission. The method which is presented relies on the evaluation of ﬂoor surface area-based ratios for
each activity, and requires the assessment of reference values to be used on the campus. As implemented, the method shows the
relative share of major uses and allows to estimate water conservation potential at the campus scale. For both electricity and water,
a special attention is paid to R&D uses, with that sector being the most signiﬁcant in terms of consumption and annual growth. 

1. Introduction
Environmental management is a growing concern for
many tertiary institutions, whether considered at the
campus scale (e.g. [1,2]), at the national scale (e.g. [3]),
or at an interregional scale (e.g. [4]), among many other
initiatives.

most generally including at least the improvement of
physical operations management or the greening of cur-
ricula [5]. The present paper is widely modiﬁed from a
lecture given at EMSU Conference in June 1999 [5].

1.1. The Ecocampus European Collaboration
Participants in the Energy–University–Environment
(EUE) Seminar [University of Bordeaux 1 (France),
March 1995], recognised that in most of their university
campuses or research laboratories, the management of
natural resources, including energy and water use, is usu-
ally based on a “laissez-faire” policy. Such a situation
was regarded by them as unwise, unfair and moreover
unaffordable, for at least two reasons:
• the ﬁnancial cost of the daily operation of teaching
and research activities continues to grow, while asso-
ciated environmental degradations are poorly taken
into account; and
• students are not receiving the best training because
of limited, out-of-date texts, bad examples in campus
buildings and isolation from others around the world
who are interested in efﬁcient building design and
protection of the environment.
Starting in 1996, the ECOCAMPUS collaboration, partly

funded by the European Commission under the THER-
MIE Programme1, had an important goal: to create a
European network of university campuses and research
laboratories whose managers, academic staff and scien-
tists, are deeply concerned by the in-house issues of sus-
tainable development. Over the past 2 years, the analysis
of data concerning electricity demand, heating energy
and water consumption has been carried out. Members
of the ECOCAMPUS collaboration were obviously com-
mitted to implementing a feasibility study in at least one
university of their own country. The collaboration
involved 14 university campuses in seven countries:
Denmark; Greece; Finland; France; Poland; Portugal;
and Romania. The main results concerning electricity
use, heating energy use, water use and waste production,
are presented in the Ecocampus ﬁnal report [6].
1.2. Ecocampus European dataset
Taken as an example from the whole Ecocampus ratio
dataset, Fig. 1 presents electricity consumption ratios
based on building ground surface areas for most of the
institutions or buildings that were studied according to
the work programme. These ratios show a variability
range of about 1–10, while water consumption ratios
range from about 1 to 30 and heating energy ratios range
from almost 1 to 9 [6]. The origin of these important

discrepancies can mostly be found: (i) in the diversity
of national-speciﬁc situations (quality of buildings, qual-
ity of distribution networks, national environment policy,
etc.); (ii) the large probability of the relative share of
different basic activities (lecturing, housing, R&D, etc.)
that can be found in the building or institution con-
cerned; and (iii), for a lesser part, in the variety in size of
buildings and institutions. Also, the lack of consumption
metering in university buildings made it difﬁcult to com-
pare homogeneous situations within the participating
universities. The present paper, focusing on electricity
and water demand, shows some of the results of the case-
study of the University of Bordeaux. For more details
about environmental management issues on the campus
of Bordeaux, a comprehensive case-study including
details of waste production is presented in Ref. [7]. An
extensive analysis of TPG campus electricity consump-
tion and load in partnership with the French electric util-
ity is given in Ref. [8].
2. General objectives and methodology
2.1. Objectives
According to the general objectives of the Ecocampus
collaboration, the goals of the present work are:
• deﬁning a methodology for auditing energy and water
uses at tertiary institutions;
• implementing and testing the methodology on the
campus of Bordeaux;
• gathering reference data to feed the Ecocampus datab-
ase; and
• using the results to gain a better knowledge of the
broad patterns of energy uses on a university campus.
Getting reference data is often troublesome due to (i)
lack of metered data; and (ii) the heterogeneity of activi-
ties that are present in an institution’s building or group
of buildings. The main goals of this paper are to discuss
the possibility of getting valuable data on an activity
basis (lecturing, housing, R&D, etc.), thus being able to
compare the energy efﬁciency of different sites bearing
in mind the respective activity share.
2.2. Methodology
The main features of the Ecocampus methodology can
be summarised as follows: (i) obtain commitment of the
top management; (ii) rely on “internal skills”, which are
widely available on university campuses, to deﬁne,
implement and support internal audits; (iii) involve stu-
dents in performing internal audits in the framework of
their curricula or research projects; (iv) consider every
accountable ﬂow on the campus.

The methodology implemented, within this broad
framework, for a demand analysis tool is brieﬂy sum-
marised in the following steps:
1. classiﬁcation
of
activities
(administration,
docu-
mentation, lecturing, R&D, housing, catering, sports);
2. a survey concerning all institutions of the campus:
water and electricity consumption; basic data (global
and per building ground surface areas, staff, number
of students, etc.);
3. evaluation of ratios for each activity: surface area-
based ratios are of great interest, because data con-
cerning building surface areas are generally central-
ised and easy to gather;
4. utilisation of ratios: ratios can be used for compara-
tive study of different sites (benchmarking), and also
for extrapolation and aggregation (aggregated con-
sumption of a given activity is obtained by combining
the total ground surface area dedicated to this activity
with the evaluated ratios); and
5. utilisation of ratios for conservation potential esti-
mation.
3. Analysis of water and electricity use at the
Talence–Pessac–Gradignan (TPG) campus
3.1. The TPG university campus
Almost all higher education activities of the Bordeaux
region are located about 6 km south downtown, in Bor-
deaux suburbs on the territories of three municipal auth-
orities: Talence; Pessac and Gradignan. With a total area
of about 2.5 km2 and a building ﬂoor area of 500 000
m2, the whole campus is one of the broadest ones in
France (Fig. 2). Each year about 50 000 students are

enrolled in one of the higher education organisations
available on the site, offering nearly all disciplinary
ﬁelds with the exception of medicine. Moreover, many
services are also available such as student restaurants
and residences, a water supply facility, post ofﬁce, cul-
ture and sports rooms, etc. As far as electricity consump-
tion and water demand are concerned, the TPG area is
equivalent to a town of 10 000 inhabitants or more.
3.1.1. Water at the TPG campus
Potable water consumption on the campus is higher
than 700 000 m3/year, not counting the geothermal water
used to heat the swimming pool (150 000 m3/year).
Water consumption, after a strong decrease in the ﬁrst
half of the 1990, is steady or slowly decreasing. Most
potable water for the campus is taken from an aquifer
regarded as overexploited in the Bordeaux area and part
of this work is supported by the Regional Water Utility
Agency2 in the framework of the local groundwater con-
servation programme. This issue is of considerable
environmental importance, since the aquifer could be
contaminated by saline water intrusion if its discharge
to the ocean keeps being reduced. Regional conservation
goals are set for the whole aquifer to save about 25%
of present exploitation. About 95% of the campus
potable water is supplied from several wells operated by
university campus facilities. As a consequence, the cost
of water supply at the campus ranges from 0.3 to 1
EURO/m3, while the average price of municipal water
in France exceeds 2 EURO/m3. Therefore, water use
could be found to be higher here than in universities fed
with municipal water. To our knowledge, water leaking
should does not signiﬁcantly affect the distribution net-
works of the campus. As a result of the survey conducted

in the present work, it appears that watering plants is a
very minor use of water on the campus. These facts
allow one to consider that water demand is driven by
activities, and that the small leakage level and watering
uses should not cause many errors in the data analysis.
3.1.2. Electricity at the TPG campus
In 1998 the overall power subscription was about 9.5
MW with the cumulated maximum power load reaching
10.3 MW; the annual electricity consumption was 25
GWh resulting in a bill of 12.7 million Francs (tax not
included) or about 2.2 million Euros. For reasons yet to
be fully investigated, electricity demand growth is high
(+8% in 1998). Electricity is supplied by EDF, the
French Electricity Utility, to >50 delivery points on the
campus. A combined heat and power (CHP) self-pro-
duction 1 MWe power plant was opened in the autumn
of 1999, illustrating a trend of some French universities,
partly induced by the deregulation of the electricity mar-
ket. Decreasing cost of electricity has been a general
trend for several years, as well as the mean increase of
electrical energy consumption on the campus. Such
increase can be partly explained by construction of new
buildings, but also by growing equipment rates, not for-
getting
the
often
increasing
unit
consumption
of
appliances. Although individual electric heaters are
present in a large number of ofﬁces on the campus, elec-
trical energy is almost never the main heating energy
source. Therefore, it is assumed that, like the water data,
the electric consumption data can be mostly explained
by activities.
3.1.3. Availability and quality of data
With about 50 electricity main meters and 60 water
main meters, supplemented by about 50 water submet-
ers, a large amount of consumption data is available. One
of the main difﬁculties is ensuring that the linkage
between the consumption data and stafﬁng or building
data is correct, so that any ratios are reliable. On the TPG
campus, which houses more than a dozen independent
institutions and particularly >30 areas of separate man-
agement — not counting at least 40 research laboratories
with a high level of autonomy — gathering such data
cannot be done without a comprehensive survey.
3.1.4. Implementation of the method at the TPG
campus
For the purpose of testing the method, the implemen-
tation was done in two steps:
Step 1: test the hypothesis of activity-driven con-
sumption and check the validity of the classiﬁcation.
Step 2: test the validity of ratios as reference data
for benchmarking and for extrapolation of uses where
consumption is not metered.
In the ﬁrst step, the most reliable data were used to
evaluate ratios for each single-activity building or insti-
tution, thus allowing one to calculate and discuss a mean
ratio per activity. Despite the large size of the TPG cam-
pus, the number of samples in each activity was often
too small to conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis
of data. In the second step, the handling of ratios for
aggregation was tested, ﬁrst on three “mini-campus”
sites and then on the whole TPG campus. The appropri-
ateness of the mean ratios from step 1 for this purpose
was discussed. An evaluation of the water conservation
potential, based on ratios per end-uses, was then conduc-
ted.
3.2. Evaluation of ratios for different “single-activity”
buildings or institutions
The sites (buildings or institutions) for which reliable
ratios could be found were classiﬁed by activity and
compared, as shown in Figs. 3 and 4. Some of the sites
could not be considered as “single-activity”, for instance
educational institutions having also catering or housing
facilities. Therefore, the classiﬁcation is more detailed
when necessary. The relevance of each type of ratio was
tested, when signiﬁcant, with a least-square regression
line (consumption versus surface area, staff, etc.) and
a coefﬁcient of determination. When it was possible, a
comparison was made between ratios based on the sur-
face area and ratios based on occupancy: however, one
must remember that, for a given type of activity, surface
area and occupancy are generally linked. Due to the dif-
ferent distribution of meters between water and elec-
tricity, fewer data were available for electricity con-
sumption and some of the ratios could not be evaluated.
These differences made a cross-analysis of water and
electricity consumption difﬁcult, so that, in many cases,
water and electricity ratios had to be treated separately.
3.2.1. Libraries
Three libraries in two large distinct buildings, and a
smaller documentation centre, are present on the cam-
pus, the overall building ground area being about 15 950
m2. With a water consumption of 2790 m3 the mean ratio
value is one of the smallest of the campus (0.17
m3/year/m2), and the surface area-based ratios appear
very homogeneous. Electricity consumption ratios show
a greater variability, but still remain among the lowest of
the campus with a mean ratio of about 25 kWh/year/m2.
3.2.2. Administration
Only one building, among those dedicated to adminis-
tration, has water and electricity meters. The ratios for
this building might provide data, for all the adminis-
tration buildings on the campus, with the orders of mag-
nitude of water consumption (0.19 m3/year/m2 and about
5.3 m3/year per staff member), and electricity consump-
tion (45 kWh/year/m2 and 1200 kWh/year per person).

3.2.3. Lecturing
3.2.3.1. Water consumption
Two subclasses are con-
sidered to discuss the relevance of ratios: single build-
ings [Fig. 3(c)], and educational institutions [Fig. 3(d)].
The ratios of single building show a very good level of
homogeneity (r2=0.98), and their mean value is probably
suitable for many other lecture halls. When considering
ratios for institutions as a whole, two points have to be
stated: (i) a slightly larger dispersion was found in the
ratios (r2=0.91), probably having two major causes.
First, structural differences do exist between the sites
and the number of students per staff member or per unit
surface may vary strongly. Second, the presence on the
sites that were investigated of other activities in variable
proportions (cafeterias, administration, etc.) may alter
the quality of ratios. As a consequence, the use of a mean
ratio should be done with care. (ii) Water consumption
of lecture buildings should be directly related to occu-
pancy, that is, to the number of students and staff, rather
than to surface area. However, ratios based on staff or
student number appear less consistent than surface area-
based ratios. Reference values could be taken as 0.2
m3/year/m2 for buildings or institutions having a low
occupancy density and 0.3 m3/year/m2 for sites with a
higher population density (for instance, <5 m2 per
student).
3.2.3.2. Electricity consumption
Due to the lack of
metered data, only educational institutions could be stud-
ied [Fig. 4(a)]. The ratios for educational institutions
show a variability range close to those of the water

ratios. However, no direct correlation is found between
water and electricity ratios. Ratios based on occupancy
were found to be less signiﬁcant. A possible explanation
is that, unlike water in this kind of buildings, electricity
consumption is better related to surface than to occu-
pancy. The mean ratio is about 41 kWh/year/m2
(r2=0.93).
3.2.4. Student housing
Ratios for housing were expected to be quite similar
on the campus where buildings and occupancy are com-
parable. This could be observed for electricity consump-
tion ratios [Fig. 4(b)], denoting a reliable mean ratio of
39 kWh/year/m2 (r2=0.96), but not for water consump-
tion ratios [Fig. 3(b)]. For most sites, water consumption
per room appears also to be large, since it might be equi-
valent to 30–60% of the mean household annual con-
sumption in the region. According to data available for
site 6, hot tap water consumption might be as high as
47% of global consumption. The values and dispersion
of ratios found on the campus seemed to indicate some
potential for water conservation, which was conﬁrmed
by a visit of the buildings concerned. As a consequence,
the mean value is probably relatively high if it is to be
used as a reference.
3.2.5. Catering
When considering ratios for catering, two categories
have a different reference data. (i) Restaurants, where
cooking is important, occupy an overall building ground
surface area >10 000 m2. (ii) Cafeterias, where often
less cooking occurs, require a smaller building surface
area, and show high surface-based ratios. For both categ-
ories, ratios per meal, although being more difﬁcult to
obtain than per surface area ones, are much more
reliable indicators.
3.2.6. Research
Research buildings or laboratories can be separated
into two main categories. (i) Buildings or laboratories
having no speciﬁc R&D equipment (geography, humani-
ties, etc.): these units only use sanitary water and ordi-
nary “commercial” building electrical energy, and the
ratios here should be close to lecturing or administration
ones. (ii) Buildings or laboratories having speciﬁc R&
D uses: most often situated in science and technology
experimental research buildings, these units showing
generally high consumption and great discrepancies need
to be considered. Water and electricity are treated separ-
ately here, because classiﬁcations do not necessarily
match: generally R&D labs often require both electricity
and water speciﬁc consumption, but some, depending on
the research ﬁeld, use just electricity (e.g. computer
science) or water (e.g. marine biology) for the R&D pur-
poses.
3.2.6.1. Water
1. For the ﬁrst category, buildings or laboratories only
have sanitary uses of water — mostly for lavatories.
Water consumption ratios per surface area are among
the lowest on the campus [Fig. 3(e)], however, there
is some variability mostly due to the heterogeneity of
a few data sets. The mean surface area-based ratio
does seem to provide a satisfactory reference value
(0.2 m3/year/m2).
2. In the case of the second category, the large disper-
sion of data is explained by the diversity of R&D uses
and heterogeneity of the equipment. All ratios [Fig.
3(f)], often ranging from 10 to 20 times the adminis-
tration or lecturing ratios, far exceed 0.2 m3/year/m2,
revealing the existence of speciﬁc R&D consumption.
The mean ratio of 3.8 m3/year/m2 is not statistically
signiﬁcant; however, being evaluated after >90% of
the surface area and consumption of R&D labora-
tories, it provides an adequate value for the whole
TPG campus.

3.2.6.2. Electricity
1. Not enough data could be obtained for research build-
ings without scientiﬁc equipment but ratios for the
known samples seem to indicate that the pattern of
consumption is quite similar to the libraries, adminis-
tration or commercial buildings.
2. Electricity consumption ratios for R&D labs are about
three to ﬁve times higher than for other buildings. A
10 times higher consumption (site 4) can be attributed
to an exceptional density of equipment. Due to the
lack of sub-metering, some results of the measure-
ment campaigns were included in the dataset. The
mean ratio (117 kWh/year/m2) has not been found
statistically signiﬁcant and care should be taken for
extrapolations after this value.
3.2.7. Sports
Due to the lack of accurate data, sports activity is not
detailed here. In particular, watering of sports grounds
may not be well known. Metered water consumption,
concerning an area of 12 700 m2 for buildings or covered
grounds, is about 16 800 m3/year, denoting a ratio of 1.3
m3/year/m2. More reliable values could be found in bet-
ter accounting of watering use, possibly related to ﬁelds
surfaces, this being out of the scope of the paper. Appar-
ent electricity use per unit of ﬂoor surface area (37
kWh/year/m2), yet to be validated, is close to that of
lecturing buildings.
3.3. Global pattern of electricity and water uses
The main goal of the aggregation is to obtain a broad
pattern of water and electricity uses on the campus,
rather than a highly accurate evaluation, in order to dis-
cuss the weight of different activities or uses in the
environmental impact of a campus.

3.3.1. Aggregation by basic activities
For almost every building on the campus, the share
of surface area dedicated to a particular activity has been
identiﬁed during the survey. Suitable ratios are combined
with the aggregated surface area of each activity to

was tested, ﬁrst on three “mini-campuses” and then on
the global campus scale, using either the mean ratios
evaluated in the previous section, or adjusted values
when the mean ratios were not signiﬁcant.
3.3.1.1. Test of aggregation for the three mini-campuses
This test was done for water ratios and concerned
three distinct “mini-campuses”, each having their own
management,
about 10 000–30 000 m2
of building
ground surface area and at least three different activities
(lecturing, housing, administration, catering or research).
The reconstructed total consumption for each site is
given in Table 1. The use of “rough” mean TPG campus
ratios may lead to adequate results but important errors
are possible [cf campus 1 (a)]. The adjustment of the
ratios, after a qualitative study, allows one to take into
account the speciﬁc aspects of each site and highly

aggregation is better for the three sites together, since
positive or negative errors should partly compensate
each other.
3.3.1.2. Aggregation for the TPG campus
When con-
sidering the ﬂoor surface areas, aggregated by activities,
lecturing, housing and R&D appear to be the most
important parts of the campus [Figs. 5 and 6(a)], for
which consumption data is known for 50–90% of the
related ﬂoor surface area. The aggregation of water and
electricity uses requires minor adjustments in the refer-
ence ratios, either because the mean ratios are statisti-
cally signiﬁcant,
or because the surface area (or
consumption) remaining to be extrapolated is small.

of every end-use. The fact that many buildings have just
one or two end-uses allows one to estimate ratios for

biology uses: open-circuit aquarium, distillation of
water, etc. Among these uses, open-circuit cooling of
scientiﬁc equipment and air conditioning are the domi-
nant ones, often with a signiﬁcant level of water spillage.
3.4. Water conservation potential
Evaluating the share of each end-use on the global
campus scale allows one to estimate the quantitatively
major uses, each of them having a different conservation
potential. Major uses at the campus are R&D and student

4. Discussion
4.1. Water and electricity proﬁles
As shown in Fig. 8, water and electricity mean ratios
denote again the importance of research uses: R&D is
the only activity being energy intensive as well as water
consuming on the TPG campus. When comparing ratios,
groups of activities appear clearly:
• low consumption density (administration, lecturing,
libraries);
• water consuming activities (housing, sports, catering);

When considering a new, as yet uninvestigated, univer-
sity site where an audit is to be implemented, knowledge
of the respective surfaces of these different activities,
although not necessarily allowing one to precisely evalu-
ate every use, may provide the orders of magnitude and
location of most of the electricity and water consump-
tion.
4.2. Conservation issues
As long as energy and water conservation are regarded
from a global point of view, most issues present many
similarities. Regarding global environmental issues at
university campuses, any important conservation poten-
tial related to R&D speciﬁc end-uses needs to be pointed
out. In order to achieve conservation potential, several
different options have been identiﬁed:
1. improved appliances (e.g. better regulation of the ﬂow
of cooling water, improvement of the standby mode
of appliances, etc.);
2. important modiﬁcation of installations (e.g. switching
to a chilled water circuit, implement remote control
on equipment, etc.); and
3. replacement of a water or electricity greedy appliance
by a more energy-efﬁcient one [9], which has been
shown to be economically feasible for part of the
existing LASER equipment in the University of Bor-
deaux 1.
A comprehensive assessment of the environmental and
ﬁnancial costs and beneﬁts of one of these options is an
issue that seems to require further development, taking
into account every relevant scale of analysis (laboratory,
university, society, market). However, two speciﬁc water
conservation aspects need to be mentioned. First, some
technical aspects of water distribution are sometimes
important and must not be neglected when focusing on
water demand: for instance, quality of networks and
leakage avoidance might be, in campuses other than
TPG, to be considered a priority. Second, at TPG cam-
pus as well as at other campuses, water is not necessary
in itself an important part of the use, that is, in most
R&D end-uses: thermal dissipation is just needed. Since
cooling production may require intensive electricity con-
sumption, an important issue lies in the comparative
evaluation of energy and environmental costs (i.e. a life-
cycle analysis, LCA) of different solutions for cooling:
non-recycled water; recycled water; chilled water; and
industrial water. This issue, obviously dependant on the
regional and global environmental impact of each
resource, would require a broader study of the links in
water and energy uses.
At the TPG campus, the low cost of water is possibly a
barrier to the achievement of conservation potential. On
a regional scale the shifting to new water resources is
expected to improve the hydrologic budget of the over-
exploited aquifer. Meanwhile, the setting up of a
regional ecotax on overexploited aquifer withdrawals,
which is likely to happen, might be a solution inducing
considerable reduction in the environmental impact of
the activities at the campus.
4.3. Discussion of the method and results
4.3.1. Appropriateness of the classiﬁcation and ratios
The classiﬁcation of activities appears to provide an
adequate description of the campus that was studied. On
campuses which would prove to be quite different from
TPG, some speciﬁc aspects might, however, require an
adaptation of the classiﬁcation. Anyway, most often
ratios were found to be relevant within a given class of
buildings,
especially
when
“generic”
activities
(education, housing, catering, libraries) were considered
with the most appropriate basis (ﬂoor surface, number
of rooms, number of meals served per year, etc.). Cases
for which an adequate correlation could not be found
should require more data to conclude about the statistical
relevance of ratios. Most generally, electricity consump-
tion ratios appear to be more homogeneous than water
consumption ratios, because minimal electric consump-
tion is required, whatever the building function is, by
very common end-uses such as: security lights; lighting;
and HVAC. For instance, ratios for housing and lectur-
ing were found to be rather similar. Higher ratios are
again found in R&D buildings where: (i) important
scientiﬁc equipment use; and (ii) speciﬁc building con-
sumption (e.g., air conditioning for experimentation
halls, air extraction and fume hoods for chemical labs,
etc.) are added to a conventional building consumption.
The situation of research is somewhat speciﬁc, and
requires that: (i) non-R&D consuming research; and (ii)
R&D consuming research should be considered separ-
ately. Ratios, as evaluated in this paper, should be suit-
able for the ﬁrst category but when considering R&D
consuming research, no proper correlation could be
found and therefore a few implications must be con-
sidered: (i) on a given campus R&D buildings should be
examined one by one; (ii) the classiﬁcation could be
further reﬁned, as to take into account subclasses such
as chemistry, experimental physics, etc., and tested on
broader samples.
4.3.2. Generalisations
Ratio-based analysis is very commonly used when
energy
or
environmental
parameters
are
studied.
Implementing such analysis requires both to gather and
process data and the reference values needed for
interpretation. From the results of the present work, it
must be underlined that:

1. Local reference values given here may not be con-
sidered, in a strict sense, as suitable to other situ-
ations, different from the campus studied (other coun-
tries, other campuses). However the method itself
appears valid, and it is also likely that some values
of ratios could be quite similar on other campuses, as
far as most generic activities are concerned.
2. As shown before, the extrapolation of consumption
on a “mini-campus” using mean ratios may require a
special care and most often a qualitative analysis. Still
it may, provided a minimal interpretation is carried
out, produce very useful indications of the environ-
mental performance of a site, as one of the ﬁrst steps
of an audit.
3. The ratio-based method can be considered as a start-
of-analysis method: the analysis of ratios gives basic
information on the environmental performance of a
site, moreover it raises many questions and generally
leads to further study of particular problems.
4. Generalisations of the method include an adaptation
for the purpose of auditing industrial sites and large
commercial zones with different activities.
4.3.3. Directions for further study
Further development of the tool can be seen to be
going in two directions: (i) on a larger scale, the method
should be implemented on a representative sample of
campuses, in order to assess reference values at the
national or European scale. (ii) At the scale of the build-
ing or appliance, end-uses and actual demand should be
investigated in order to assess best values rather than
mean values to be referred at when examining ratios.
Such work has been ongoing at University of Bordeaux
for several years, focusing on the characterisation of
equipment actual demand. It aims to increase the knowl-
edge and to help deﬁne improvement strategies (labelling
of appliances, subsidisation programmes).
5. Conclusion
As a part of the extensive case-study of the university
campus of Bordeaux, conducted in the framework of the
Ecocampus European collaboration, a tool for assessing
some indicators of environmental performance has been
implemented and successfully tested on the TPG cam-
pus. Although the method could be further tested and
improved, on a larger scale, the guideline shown in the
present paper may be useful for managers or researchers
who regard best management of the physical and
environmental parameters as one of the necessary
elements of an outstanding environmental policy at their
university. Especially, a larger number of physical ﬂows
should be taken into account: for instance, the ﬂow of
waste, not forgetting chemical waste and wastewater,
which have also been studied at the University of Bor-
deaux. Nevertheless the method that has been presented
in this paper is just a tool, and it should be understood
as a simple element of a comprehensive environmental
management system. But the authors do believe that
environmental
management
at
universities
must
include — yet should not be restricted to — a compre-
hensive and powerful analysis of every accountable ﬂow
on a campus, which should:
1. be based on physical units, however also allowing
economical matters to be considered;
2. include the assessment of consistent indicators;
3. involve the detailed study of these indicators in order
to understand and estimate the actual potential of
improvement of the system; and
4. suit a continuous improvement of the environmental
parameters of the system, according to the exemplary
environmental friendliness that tertiary institutions
have to demonstrate.
As a conclusion, an affordable sustainable development
policy for universities might involve at least the
measurement of the impact, the deﬁnition of a set of
visible improvements, and also induce money savings as
an incentive. Extra beneﬁts of such a policy are not by-
products but essential goals:
1. more adequate training of students to energy and
environmental issues; and
2. extending
R&D
activities
(waste
management,
LCA, etc.).
Or in other words two fundamental elements of a cleaner
scientiﬁc process.
